summary: Background: Discriminating mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from subjective cognitive decline (SCD), and healthy controls (HC) remains challenging. Digital tools may overcome paper-and-pencil screening’s limitations. Objective: This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and usability of CogniPaz (Daniel Blanco), an ecologically oriented, mobile health (mHealth), gamified cognitive assessment tool exploring memory and executive functions, in discriminating MCI (particularly amnestic phenotypes [aMCI]) from SCD, and HC. Methods: This prospective observational study recruited a convenience sample of consecutive patients with cognitive complaints and HC at La Paz University Hospital Cognitive Disorders Unit from April 2025 to January 2026. Demographic and clinical characteristics, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores were collected. An evaluator blinded to the MoCA scores oversaw the automated, self-administered CogniPaz assessment. Participants were classified into HC (no cognitive complaints, MoCA score≥26), SCD (cognitive complaints, MoCA score≥26), and MCI (cognitive complaints without functional impairment, MoCA score<26, subdivided into amnestic [aMCI] and nonamnestic phenotypes). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses using age-adjusted models, the DeLong test, and bootstrap validation evaluated diagnostic accuracy across groups. The correlation between MoCA and CogniPaz scores was assessed using Spearman rank correlation. Participants with available biomarker data underwent exploratory analysis of CogniPaz’s ability to detect biologically confirmed any-cause neurodegeneration (bND). Usability was tested using an ad hoc Likert questionnaire (1‐9 points). Results: The participants (n=84, 57.1% female; median age 72.0, IQR 62.5-77.0 years) included 27 HC, 17 with SCD, 22 with aMCI, and 18 with nonamnestic MCI. The aMCI group was older than the SCD group (age: median 76.5, IQR 70.8-78.8 vs median 59.0, IQR 50.0-69.0 years; Kruskal-Wallis/Dunn, =.003). CogniPaz scores correlated with MoCA scores (ρ0.81, 95% CI 0.75‐0.89; .001). CogniPaz showed good concurrent accuracy, independently of age: MCI vs HC (area under the curve [AUC]=0.880, 95% CI 0.798‐0.961), MCI vs SCD (AUC=0.915, 95% CI 0.841‐0.990), aMCI vs HC (AUC=0.910, 95% CI 0.830‐0.990), and aMCI vs SCD (AUC=0.943, 95% CI 0.878‐1.000). At the provisional <28.5 cutoff point, sensitivity ranged from 85.0% (34/40, 95% CI 70.2‐94.3) to 90.9% (20/22, 95% CI 70.8‐98.9) and specificity from 74.1% (20/27, 95% CI 53.7‐88.9) to 82.4% (14/17, 95% CI 56.6‐96.2) across comparisons. CogniPaz suggested capacity to detect bND (AUC=0.810, 95% CI 0.661‐0.958), with potential incremental value over MoCA and age (odds ratio [OR]=0.78, 95% CI 0.60‐0.94; =.02). Median administration time was 9.39 (IQR 7.53‐11.38) minutes with 100% (84/84) completion. User satisfaction was high (median score 8.4/9, IQR 7.9‐8.6; Cronbach α=0.84). Conclusions: CogniPaz is an innovative, user-friendly mHealth tool that addresses classical cognitive screening tools’ limitations through a brief, multidomain, minimally supervised gamified format, with high patient acceptance. It correlates with MoCA scores, shows good concurrent capacity to differentiate MCI, particularly aMCI, from SCD and HC, and appears promising for identifying bND. Pending external longitudinal validation, these findings support CogniPaz as a candidate for early cognitive screening in primary care.
title: CogniPaz, an Ecologically Oriented Gamified mHealth Tool for Detecting Mild Cognitive Impairment: Prospective Cohort Diagnostic Accuracy Study

summary: Background: Early childhood caries (ECC) is a prevalent yet preventable disease that significantly impacts young children’s health and quality of life. The World Health Organization’s highlights the potential of mobile health programs to enhance engagement and support sustained oral health behavior change. Objective: The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of the SmilesUp 12-week SMS text messaging–based education and support program to improve parents’ management of their children’s oral health behaviors compared to standard clinical care. Methods: We conducted a multisite, assessor-blinded, parallel-design randomized controlled trial among parents of children aged 0 to 6 years who had an ECC diagnosis and attended 1 of 6 public dental clinics in metropolitan, regional, and rural New South Wales, Australia. Participants were randomly assigned to either an intervention group receiving the fully automated 12-week SmilesUp program (3 SMS text messages weekly) or a control group. Both groups continued to receive usual standard dental clinical treatment. The primary behavioral outcome was parent-reported twice-daily toothbrushing with fluoride toothpaste. Secondary outcomes included adherence to oral health–promoting bedtime routines and child consumption of sugar-sweetened foods and beverages. Oral health self-efficacy was measured using 6 behavioral theory–mapped items across oral hygiene, diet, and bedtime routines. Results: A total of 154 participants were enrolled and randomized (n=78, 50.6% in the control group; n=76, 49.4% in the intervention group) across 6 sites, with 80.5% (124/154) completing the follow-up assessment. High program adherence was observed, with 96.1% (73/76) of intervention participants completing the program. At 12 weeks, a greater proportion of SmilesUp participants reported brushing their children’s teeth twice daily (45/61, 73.8% vs 42/63, 66.7%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.45, 95% CI 0.95-6.74; =.07), though this difference was not statistically significant. Significant improvements were observed in adherence to bedtime routines (54/61, 88.5% vs 45/63, 71.4%; aOR 3.25, 95% CI 1.15-10.18; =.03) as well as oral health knowledge on toothbrushing (46/50, 92.0% vs 41/52, 78.8%; aOR 5.47, 95% CI 1.48-25.19; =.02). No statistically significant differences were found in sugar-sweetened food (10/61, 16.4% vs 4/63, 6.3%; aOR 3.72, 95% CI 1.02-17.14; =.06) or beverage (25/61, 41.0% vs. 27/63, 42.9%; aOR 1.08, 95% CI 0.49-2.30; =.85) consumption. Conclusions: These findings suggest that co-designed SMS text messaging–based programs show promise and may represent a feasible strategy for oral health behavior change. However, larger-scale and longer-term studies are needed to confirm sustained effectiveness using clinical outcomes. Future research should also explore ways mobile health can be scaled and cost-effectively embedded into comprehensive, interdisciplinary primary models of care. Trial Registration: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12623000325606; https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12623000325606 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.1371/journal.pone.0310561
title: Co-Designed Text Messaging Intervention for Parents of Children With Early Childhood Caries: Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: Chronic disease and comorbid mental health problems disproportionately affect rural and underserved populations. Digital self-management programs are potentially scalable, but evaluations often focus on narrow outcomes. Objective: This study examined 12-month longitudinal changes in psychological and multidomain outcomes among Pictou County Patient Empowerment Program participants and explored co-occurring changes and psychological moderators. Methods: This single-arm prospective interventional study enrolled 182 community-dwelling adults with ≥1 chronic condition in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, between October 2023 and August 2025 through community-based outreach. Median age was 60 (IQR 51‐68) years, 155 of 182 (85.2%) participants were women, and the median number of chronic conditions was 3 (IQR 1‐3). The initial 6-month digital intervention delivered brief daily modules targeting physical activity, nutrition, stress regulation, sleep, habit formation, and social connection, followed by a 6-month lower-intensity maintenance period during which monthly group videoconference sessions continued to be offered. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. Primary outcomes were illness perceptions (Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire), perceived stress (10-item Perceived Stress Scale [PSS-10]), disease-related worry (10-item Questionnaire on Distress in Cancer Patients), life satisfaction (Satisfaction With Life Scale), and mental well-being (World Health Organization-Five Well-Being Index [WHO-5]). Secondary outcomes assessed the physical, behavioral, and psychosocial domains. Generalized estimating equations estimated population-averaged longitudinal changes, adjusted for age, sex, relationship status, comorbidity burden, and baseline depression or anxiety medication use. Exploratory models examined co-occurring changes and moderation. Tests were 2-sided with =.05. Results: Across outcomes and follow-up assessments, completion ranged from 58.2% (95% CI 51.0%-65.2%; 106/182) to 65.4% (95% CI 58.2%‐71.9%; 119/182). At 12 months, illness perceptions decreased (β=−7.3, 95% CI −9.7 to −4.9), perceived stress decreased (β=−2.4, 95% CI −3.5 to −1.3), disease-related worry decreased (β=−6.3, 95% CI −7.8 to −4.7), life satisfaction increased (β=2.5, 95% CI 1.4‐3.5), and mental well-being increased (β=10.4, 95% CI 7.2‐13.5; all <.001). Secondary outcomes improved across fatigue, sleep, diet quality, sedentary behavior, spiritual well-being, mental health–related quality of life, weight, and BMI. Exploratory analyses showed that improvements in fatigue, sleep quality, and illness perceptions co-occurred with greater well-being and life satisfaction and lower perceived stress and disease-related worry at both follow-up assessment points. Clinically meaningful stress improvement (≥4-point PSS-10 reduction) was achieved by 36.4% (95% CI 27.3%-45.6%, 39/107) and 43.4% (95% CI 34.0%-52.8%, 46/106) participants at 6 and 12 months, respectively. At 12 months, 43.5% (95% CI 34.2%-52.9%, 47/108) participants reported clinically meaningful improvement in mental well-being (≥10-point WHO-5 increase). Conclusions: Participation in this low-bandwidth, home-based digital self-management program was associated with sustained psychological, physical, and behavioral improvements among rural adults with chronic conditions. These multidomain findings support randomized controlled evaluation of scalable digital self-management approaches as adjuncts to rural chronic disease care. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06064110; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06064110
title: Multidomain Outcomes of a Digital Self-Management Program in Rural Adults With Chronic Conditions: Single-Arm Prospective Interventional Study

summary: Background: Recovery after total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is typically assessed with infrequent clinic-based evaluations that may not reflect patients’ everyday mobility. Smartphone inertial sensors enable scalable, repeated gait measurement in real-world settings, but the extent to which prompted walking tests reflect daily life walking during recovery is not well defined. Objective: The objective of this study was to characterize week-by-week recovery trajectories after THA and TKA using high-frequency smartphone sensor data and quantify the difference between prompted in-app walking tests and passive daily life background walking. Methods: We analyzed longitudinal smartphone-based gait measurements from 735 patients (THA, n=350; TKA, n=385) who underwent unilateral surgery between July 2022 and October 2025. Nine spatiotemporal gait parameters were monitored over the first 15 postoperative weeks across 2 conditions: prompted “in-app” walks and passively captured “background” walks. Recovery trajectories were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier time-to-baseline analyses, linear mixed-effects models, and comparison of late-stage plateau levels (weeks 11‐15) using estimated marginal means of the models. Results: Across all parameters, THA patients returned to preoperative baseline levels faster than TKA patients, with mean trajectories generally approaching baseline by week 4 for THA versus weeks 6 to 8 for TKA. Linear mixed-effects models showed that surgical procedure type significantly influenced recovery trajectory for all parameters except single support of the unaffected leg. All gait parameters except stance asymmetry and single support of the unaffected leg exhibited persistent differences through the late-recovery plateau (weeks 11‐15). We also compared prompted “in-app” walks with passively captured background walking. Prompted and passive walking showed systematic divergence in both THA and TKA; prompted assessments generally indicated faster or more complete return to baseline than passive daily life walking. Finally, preoperative gait level was strongly associated with postoperative trajectories, with baseline-stratified analyses showing distinct patterns of recovery between groups. Conclusions: High-frequency smartphone gait assessment quantifies procedure-specific recovery dynamics and demonstrates that prompted tests and passive daily life measurements capture distinct, noninterchangeable functional signals. Parameters from prompted walks plateaued while those from passively captured walks were still changing; prompted testing alone therefore captures only one component of returning function, highlighting the additional information that passive, real-world gait monitoring can provide.
title: Real-World Functional Gait Recovery Trajectories After Total Hip and Total Knee Arthroplasty via Smartphone Sensors: Observational Longitudinal Study

summary: Background: Prenatal depression and anxiety have emerged as pressing global public health challenges. In the digital era, excessive smartphone use may exert complex effects on maternal mental health. Prior research has predominantly focused on adolescents, whereas evidence among pregnant women, particularly regarding total weekly use and use during critical circadian windows, such as after waking and before bedtime, remains limited. Furthermore, the mediating role of sleep quality in these associations has yet to be systematically examined. Objective: This study aimed to investigate the associations of smartphone addiction and time-specific smartphone use with prenatal depression and anxiety, and to assess the mediating role of sleep quality in these associations. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study enrolled 537 pregnant women. Smartphone use characteristics, sleep quality, and prenatal depression and anxiety were assessed using the Smartphone Addiction Scale-Short Version (SAS-SV), objective total weekly smartphone use recorded by the device, and self-reported duration of smartphone use after waking and duration of bedtime smartphone use; the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), respectively. Binary logistic regression was used to estimate associations, restricted cubic spline (RCS) models were used to explore nonlinear patterns, and exploratory mediation analyses were used to examine whether sleep quality statistically accounted for part of the observed associations. Results: The prevalence of moderate-to-severe prenatal depression and anxiety was 8.8% (47/537) and 5.8% (31/537), respectively. After adjusting for covariates, smartphone addiction was associated with higher odds of depression (odds ratio [OR] 3.461, 95% CI 1.771‐7.100) and anxiety (OR 7.738, 95% CI 3.064‐23.172). Duration of smartphone use after waking ≥61 minutes and duration of bedtime smartphone use ≥91 minutes were also associated with higher odds of affective disorders. RCS analyses further revealed distinct nonlinear patterns across different exposure dimensions: duration of smartphone use after waking displayed U-shaped and J-shaped associations with depression and anxiety, respectively, while total weekly use displayed a U-shaped association with anxiety. Exploratory mediation analyses showed that the indirect pathways through sleep quality were statistically significant for the associations of bedtime smartphone use, weekly smartphone use, and smartphone addiction with prenatal depression, with mediation proportions of 44.89% (0.0065/0.0145), 31.30% (0.0056/0.0183), and 31.48% (0.0415/0.1315), respectively. The corresponding proportions in the anxiety models were 35.83% (0.0044/0.0123), 27.05% (0.0039/0.0144), and 22.73% (0.0271/0.1187). Conclusions: Smartphone addiction and excessive smartphone use after waking and before bedtime were associated with higher odds of prenatal depression and anxiety. Sleep quality may statistically account for part of these associations, but longitudinal studies are needed to establish temporal ordering and causal pathways.
title: The Mediating Role of Sleep Quality in Associations of Smartphone Addiction and Time-Specific Use With Prenatal Depression and Anxiety: Cross-Sectional Observational Study

summary: Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide, yet participation in cardiac rehabilitation (CR) remains suboptimal. Wrist-worn wearables may support fully remote or hybrid CR through activity monitoring and individualized feedback, but the effectiveness and consistency of benefits remain uncertain. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of wrist-worn wearable–guided CR delivered through fully remote or hybrid programs initiated during phase II or III CR in patients with CVD. Methods: A total of 8 databases were searched for randomized controlled trials published from January 1, 2015, through August 7, 2026. Eligible trials enrolled adults with CVD and integrated a wrist-worn wearable into fully remote or hybrid CR. Studies focused primarily on heart failure or using wearables only for outcome measurement were excluded. Primary outcomes were peak oxygen consumption (VO<sub>2</sub>), 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), and daily steps. Random-effects meta-analyses used mean differences (MDs), except for quality of life, which used standardized MDs. Between-study variance was estimated using the DerSimonian-Laird method, pooled-effect CIs used the Knapp-Hartung adjustment, and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) used the Nagashima-Noma-Furukawa parametric bootstrap method. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane Risk of Bias 2. Subgroup and univariable meta-regression analyses explored study and intervention characteristics. Results: A total of 18 trials involving 1993 randomized participants, reported in 20 publications, were included; 17 contributed to meta-analysis. Pooled estimates favored wearable-guided CR for peak VO<sub>2</sub> (10 studies; 591 participants; MD 1.69, 95% CI 0.46-2.92, 95% PI –2.21 to 5.39 mL/kg/min), 6MWD (9 studies; 1094 participants; MD 31.03, 95% CI 7.66-53.92, 95% PI –62.11 to 123.18 m), and daily steps (8 studies; 474 participants; MD 1062.8, 95% CI 383.5-1825.0, 95% PI –503.0 to 2860.0 steps/day). All 3 PIs included the null, indicating uncertainty about consistency across future comparable settings. No clear pooled effects were observed for anaerobic threshold, BMI, waist circumference, grip strength, or quality of life. Subgroup differences were not statistically significant. In univariable meta-regression, a higher proportion of female participants was associated with greater peak VO<sub>2</sub> improvement, although this aggregate-level finding was exploratory. Conclusions: Wrist-worn wearable–guided CR delivered through fully remote or hybrid programs may improve average exercise capacity and physical activity in patients with CVD. However, PIs included the null, indicating uncertainty about consistency across future settings. These programs may extend activity monitoring, individualized feedback, and behavioral support beyond center-based CR, but their multicomponent nature prevents attributing effects to wearables alone. Larger, rigorously designed trials with standardized protocols and outcomes should identify the patients and program components most likely to benefit. Future research should also evaluate long-term adherence, safety, equity, and implementation within routine multidisciplinary CR across diverse health systems.
title: Effectiveness of Wrist-Worn Wearable–Guided Cardiac Rehabilitation Delivered Through Fully Remote or Hybrid Programs in Patients With Cardiovascular Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

summary: Background: Mobile health (mHealth) apps have become important tools for HIV/AIDS management. Although the Mobile App Rating Scale and its user version are widely used, how different stakeholder groups combine quality dimensions into overall judgments remains unclear. Discrepancies between researcher and patient evaluations may affect app adoption and clinical effectiveness. Objective: This exploratory study aimed to compare configurational pathways associated with high subjective quality ratings of HIV/AIDS apps between researchers and patients using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. Methods: Twenty-one Chinese HIV/AIDS mobile apps from early 2023 were evaluated by 3 researchers using the original Mobile App Rating Scale and 2 HIV-positive patients using the user version of the Mobile App Rating Scale. Six conditions were examined: engagement, functionality, aesthetics, information quality, privacy protection, and developer type. Necessary and sufficient configurations were identified for both groups. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests compared raw ratings between groups. Sensitivity analyses covered 4 calibration anchor sets, 4 raw-consistency cutoffs, 4 proportional reduction in inconsistency cutoffs, and multivalue operationalization of privacy protection. Results: Researcher and patient ratings differed significantly for functionality (median difference 0.50, IQR 0.00 to 0.63; P=.003) and engagement (−0.20, IQR −0.40 to 0.10; P=.04), but not for aesthetics (P=.16), information (P=.07), or subjective quality (P=.06). Five sufficient configurations were identified for researchers (solution consistency=0.981, coverage=0.649) and 4 for patients (solution consistency=0.998, coverage=0.796). Configurations including privacy protection appeared only among researchers; its absence appeared in 3 patient configurations, reflecting the rarity of protection in the sample (5/21 apps) rather than lower patient ratings for protected apps. For patients, functionality (0.907) and information quality (0.915) exceeded the necessity threshold but were strongly correlated (r=0.816), so functionality was retained on substantive grounds rather than as an independent necessary condition. Illustrative cases were Wu Ai Fang Hua and Ai Yi Jian for the researcher-oriented pathway and Chabei for the patient-oriented pathway. Sensitivity analyses left the configurations unchanged across all anchor sets and raw-consistency cutoffs; 1 researcher configuration did not survive the stricter proportional reduction in inconsistency cutoffs, and the patient necessity result was anchor-dependent. Conclusions: The 2 evaluator panels’ assessments of HIV/AIDS mHealth apps appeared to follow different configurational logic in this sample, with several equifinal pathways to high subjective quality in each group. Because the patient panel comprised 2 evaluators, and 21 apps were analyzed with 6 conditions, the findings should be read as hypothesis-generating rather than representative of people living with HIV. The findings nonetheless suggest that both expert and end-user perspectives are needed during mHealth development, and that, because privacy protection was rare and not required for a favorable patient judgment, its provision in a population highly vulnerable to disclosure-related harm needs to be ensured by developers and regulators rather than left to user demand.
title: Configurations of Quality Dimensions Associated With Researcher and Patient Ratings of HIV/AIDS Mobile Health Apps in China: Fuzzy-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis

summary: Background: AI-based tools for oral cancer screening have shown promising performance in curated image datasets, but their performance in real-world mobile community screening workflows remains less clear. Objective: This study evaluated the prospective field performance of a parameter-locked, mobile AI-assisted oral lesion triage system embedded in a human-supervised community oral cancer screening workflow. Methods: We conducted a prospective community-based field evaluation in eastern Taiwan from June 17 to December 31, 2025. Trained nonspecialist personnel acquired standard white-light intraoral images using handheld mobile devices during routine screening. The AI system incorporated on-site image quality assessment and lesion-level risk stratification into green, yellow, and red triage categories. Technically inadequate images after repeated acquisition attempts were classified as ungradable and excluded from performance analysis. Three board-certified oral and maxillofacial specialists established an operational clinical reference standard through structured image review and consensus adjudication. The primary outcome was lesion-level identification of high-risk lesions requiring specialist referral, defined as red versus nonred triage. Diagnostic performance was estimated with Wilson 95% CIs; precision-recall performance and preconsensus specialist agreement were also assessed. Results: Among 602 screened participants, 4283 interpretable intraoral images were included in expert adjudication and lesion-level analysis. The AI system flagged 68 red lesions; 12 (17.6%) were confirmed as high risk, and 4 additional high-risk lesions were identified during expert review, yielding 16 high-risk events for the primary red-triage analysis. For high-risk lesion identification, sensitivity was 75% (12/16; 95% CI 50.5%-89.8%) and positive predictive value was 17.6% (12/68; 95% CI 10.4%-28.4%); specificity, negative predictive value, and accuracy were 98.6% (3928/3984), 99.9% (3928/3932), and 98.5% (3940/4000), respectively. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values were 0.957 for red, 0.931 for yellow, and 0.964 for green triage; precision-recall analysis showed area under the precision-recall curve values of 0.8235, 0.9052, and 0.9476, respectively. Preconsensus specialist agreement was high, with a Fleiss κ of 0.921 and a Gwet AC1 of 0.981. Conclusions: This mobile AI-assisted oral lesion triage system was feasibly integrated into a real-world community screening workflow operated by trained nonspecialist personnel. In this low-prevalence field setting, red triage showed moderate sensitivity and modest positive predictive value, supporting its use as human-supervised referral-prioritization support rather than autonomous diagnosis. Further multicenter studies with blinded assessment, participant-level outcomes, workflow-efficiency measures, and longitudinal follow-up are needed before clinical impact and scalability can be determined.
title: Mobile AI-Assisted Oral Lesion Triage for Community Oral Cancer Screening: Prospective Field Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Telemedicine has emerged as a critical strategy to address health care access gaps in hard-to-reach areas, particularly in resource-constrained settings. While telemedicine services have expanded across India, evidence on post-implementation experiences, specifically regarding the integration of portable diagnostic tools, and the assisting role of frontline health care workers, remains limited. Understanding these sociotechnical dynamics is essential for optimizing digital health interventions in remote areas. Objective: This study aimed to explore perceptions, experiences, and implementation processes of an assisted telemedicine model where frontline health care workers facilitate real-time, doorstep patient-assisted-to-doctor consultations using portable diagnostics and a customized portal among health care workers and patients in hard-to-reach villages of Rajasthan, India. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted in 5 remote villages of Balotra district, Rajasthan, between December 2025 and January 2026, following a 10-month telemedicine intervention. In-depth, semistructured interviews were conducted with 28 participants, including medical officers (n=3, 10.71%), nurses, and accredited social health activists or auxiliary nurse midwives (n=10, 35.71%), and patients (n=15, 53.57%). Cadre-specific semistructured interview guides were developed using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and Technology Acceptance Model. Interviews were analyzed using a reflexive thematic analysis approach, incorporating both inductive and deductive coding approaches in NVivo 15 (Lumivero). Triangulation across participant groups and analytic perspectives was used to enhance credibility and trustworthiness. Results: The analysis revealed that the assisted telemedicine model fundamentally reconfigured treatment-seeking behavior by providing doorstep care, significantly reducing travel burdens, and out-of-pocket expenditures. Frontline health care workers acted as crucial sociotechnical mediators, bridging the digital divide and fostering patient trust, particularly among women and older adults. Health care providers reported increased clinical confidence and workflow efficiency, supported by real-time vital monitoring and cross-verification via digital chatbots. However, implementation was challenged by intermittent network connectivity, diagnostic limitations for conditions requiring physical palpation, and occasional stock-outs of essential medicines. Despite these barriers, the gradual acceptance of the system was heavily facilitated by the continuous engagement and cultural mediation of local health workers. Conclusions: Telemedicine was perceived as a feasible and acceptable model for extending primary health care services in hard-to-reach areas, provided it is embedded within an assisted model supported by trained frontline workers and responsive technical systems. The findings emphasize the need to shift health care policy toward mediated-digital models, formally recognizing community health workers as digital health navigators. Future scale-up must prioritize strengthening rural digital infrastructure and ensuring a reliable supply chain for essential medicines to sustain long-term engagement and health equity. Trial Registration: Clinical Trials Registry—India (CTRI) CTRI/2024/10/076070; https://tinyurl.com/yr952847 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/92996
title: Insights on Postimplementation and Delivery of Telemedicine in Remote Areas of Rajasthan: Qualitative Study

summary: Background: Adolescents living with perinatally acquired HIV (PHIV) remain at risk of neurocognitive difficulties, yet access to valid neurocognitive tests is limited in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where most of this population resides. Tests that can be administered by nonspecialist personnel are culturally and linguistically appropriate for SSA’s diverse populations and are brief enough for routine use are needed to expand access, but few such tools exist. Objective: We adapted , a brief tablet-based neurocognitive test battery, into Luganda and evaluated its validity and acceptability for use among Ugandan adolescents with PHIV. Methods: In this cross-sectional validation study, 100 Ugandan adolescents aged 11 to 20 years (50 with PHIV; 50 HIV-negative controls) completed the Luganda- or English-language battery and a commonly used traditional test battery. Participants were recruited from an existing longitudinal cardiovascular cohort at the Joint Clinical Research Centre in Kampala, Uganda. We examined convergent validity with correlations between the 2 batteries’ individual and global -scores, known-groups validity with unadjusted and age-adjusted group comparisons, criterion validity by examining classification agreement between the 2 batteries quantified with Cohen κ, and acceptability through self-reported technology use and ease of use. Results: and the traditional battery global -scores were strongly correlated (=0.75; <.001). Correlations between tests assessing similar domains were generally small to moderate, and were strongest for processing speed, attention, and working memory. Adolescents with PHIV scored significantly lower than controls on global scores for both (=.008) and the traditional battery (=.003), even after adjusting for age. Agreement between batteries in classifying participants ≤1 SD (κ=0.56) and ≤2 SD (κ=0.66) below the global -score mean was moderate, with both batteries classifying more adolescents with PHIV than controls below these thresholds. Although fewer than half of participants (42/97, 43%) had previously used a tablet, most rated as easy to use, and prior tablet experience was not independently associated with performance after age adjustment. Conclusions: The Luganda-adapted demonstrated convergent, known-groups, and criterion validity in Ugandan adolescents with PHIV. By delivering automated administration, automated scoring, and standardized multimedia instructions in the local language on a portable tablet, addresses several persistent barriers to neurocognitive assessment in low-resource settings, including shortages of specialist personnel, the time burden of traditional batteries, and the scarcity of culturally and linguistically appropriate tools. The battery was found to be highly acceptable among adolescents with little or no prior tablet experience. These findings add to a growing body of evidence supporting tablet-based assessment as a practical and scalable mobile health approach to expanding access to neurocognitive testing. Future research should evaluate test-retest reliability, sensitivity to change over time, normative benchmarks, and implementation within real-world clinical workflows.
title: Tablet-Based Neurocognitive Tests for Ugandan Adolescents Living With HIV: Cross-Sectional Validation Study
